title: Cyperus compressus: How to Identify and Control This Annual Sedge
metaTitle: Cyperus compressus in Rice: Annual Sedge ID and Control
metaDescription: Cyperus compressus, called gisai kalabaw or tuhog dalag, grows in lowland rice. Learn to spot its flat green spikelets and weed it before it seeds.
excerpt: Cyperus compressus, the annual sedge, forms dense tufts in irrigated and rainfed lowland rice fields in the Philippines. Farmers call it gisai kalabaw or tuhog dalag. It grows from seed and lives for only one season. This page shows you how to spot its flat, greenish spikelets and how to control it before it drops seed.

heroImage.alt: Annual sedge (Cyperus compressus), a sedge weed of Philippine rice fields
heroImage.credit: Sun Jiao (Interaccoonale), CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

blocks.text:
This damo is a sedge from the Cyperaceae family. Its English name is annual sedge, while farmers in the provinces know it as gisai kalabaw or tuhog dalag. Cyperus compressus grows in both irrigated and rainfed lowland rice fields.

As its English name says, it is an annual. It sprouts, flowers and dies within one season. It spreads by seed only, so every plant you let flower adds new seeds to the soil. Those seeds wait for the next land preparation, then sprout with the new crop. That is why early weeding pays off with this sedge. If you clear it before it flowers, you cut off the next generation at the source. A few minutes of hand weeding now can save you hours later.

blocks.caption: Quick facts about Cyperus compressus
rows: Irrigated and rainfed lowland rice fields

blocks.text: Like all sedges, it has a solid, three sided stem with no nodes, unlike the round, hollow stem of rice. The stems are smooth and green, and many of them grow in a dense tuft from one base. Its leaves stay shorter than the stems. At the top, the flower head looks simple and open. Each spike holds 3 to 10 flat, greenish spikelets crowded together like fingers.

items: Dense tufts of smooth, green stems rising together from a single base.
Leaves that stay shorter than the flowering stems, so the heads stand above them.
An open, simple flower head instead of a tight, round ball.
Spikes with 3 to 10 crowded spikelets spread out like the fingers of a hand.
Greenish spikelets that look very flat, as if pressed between the pages of a book.

blocks.text:
Like other sedges, Cyperus compressus competes with your palay for light, water and fertilizer. Its dense tufts take up room between the rice hills, and its roots draw on the same nutrients. If it sprouts together with the crop, young rice plants feel that pressure the most.

Because it is an annual, it relies on seed to come back. Every plant left to flower adds seed to the soil, so the problem grows each season. Its seeds can also end up in harvested palay and lower the quality of seed you keep. Thick patches give shelter to insect pests near the rice hills, too.

items: Pull the tufts by hand while they are young and before the flat spikelets ripen, since it spreads only by seed.
Level the field well and keep water over the soil after planting, so its seeds have fewer dry spots to sprout in.
Weed the bunds and dry corners too, so no plant there drops seed back into the paddy.

blocks.text: What to Do at Each Age of Your Rice

items: **0 to 5 days:** keep the soil saturated. Use a pre emergence herbicide only if the field had many weeds last season.
**6 to 10 days:** hand weed in transplanted rice. In direct seeded rice, this is the window for an early post emergence spray.
**11 to 20 days:** keep water in the field, weed by hand or with a rotary weeder, and let Azolla and the Altica beetle help. Spray only if those fail.
**21 to 30 days:** top up the water and keep weeding. Spray only if weeding fails.
**31 to 40 days (transplanted rice):** hand weed. A spray this late is only a rescue.
After any post emergence spray, bring the water back within 1 to 3 days at 3 to 5 cm and hold it for 4 to 5 days. Keep young rice above it.

blocks.text: Active Ingredients That Work on Sedges

If water and weeding cannot hold Cyperus compressus down, choose an active ingredient that works on sedges at the age of your rice. The table follows the PhilRice eDamuhan recommendations. Shop by the ingredient on the label, never by the brand. If your field also has other kinds of weeds, the [weed control helper](/weeds#control) finds the ingredients that cover all of them.

blocks.text: Use only herbicides registered with the [Fertilizer and Pesticide Authority](/blog/fertilizer-and-pesticide-authority), and follow the label on the pack: the rate, the timing, the water and the protective clothing. Switch herbicide groups between seasons so the weeds do not learn to survive them. Our [guide to herbicides for rice](/weeds/herbicides-for-rice-weeds) explains the groups.
Keep Cyperus compressus Out Next Season

items: Plant clean, certified seed. Weed seeds mixed into the punla are the easiest way in.
Keep the seedbed, the canals and the bunds free of weeds, so seed does not wash or blow into the paddy.
Prepare the land well: flood, plow, let the weed seeds sprout, then kill them when you harrow. Level the field so water covers it evenly.
Pull escapes before their flower clusters turn brown, since one clump drops a great deal of tiny seed.
Keep the field clean after harvest and through the fallow, so fewer seeds build up in the soil for next season.

blocks.text: These steps work for every [sedge weed](/weeds/types-of-weeds) in the paddy, not only this one. The [weed management guide](/weeds/weed-management-in-rice) puts them in order for a whole season.
Not Sure It Is Cyperus compressus?

Take a clear photo of the leaf, the stem and the flower or seed head, then ask [Anee, the smart farm technician](/features/ai-agricultural-technician) in anee.io, in Tagalog or English. Anee tells you which weed it most likely is, its group, and what to do at the age of your rice. blocks.text: Questions Farmers Ask About Cyperus compressus

items.q: What do Filipino farmers call Cyperus compressus?
items.a: Filipino farmers call it gisai kalabaw or tuhog dalag. In English it goes by annual sedge, because it lives for only one season. It belongs to the sedge family, Cyperaceae. If you are not sure you have the right weed, check for flat, greenish spikelets in finger like clusters at the top of the stem.

items.q: How do I control it in my rice field?
items.a: Start with clean seed and a well leveled field. Then keep a steady layer of water so fewer seeds sprout. Pull young tufts by hand before they flower, and check again a few weeks later. If you need a herbicide, choose one that works on sedges and fits the age of your rice. Always follow the FPA registered label.

items.q: Is annual sedge harmful to palay?
items.a: Yes. Even though it lives only one season, it competes with rice for light, water and fertilizer while it grows. It also leaves seeds behind, so a few plants this season can become many next season. Its seeds can mix with harvested grain too. Weeding it early keeps that harm small and saves work later.
